verdict.reasoning: Patient reports left elbow swelling for about a week and that it is not painful: "about a week ago... weird swelling on my elbow... It's not painful at all." and confirms it is the left elbow.
Patient describes warmth and fluid sensation: "it's slightly warm, and I kind of feel like it's a bit fluid inside" at the left elbow.
Patient denies trauma: Doctor asks, "have you banged that elbow? Did you have any kind of injury?" Patient: "No, not really. Not that I know of. I haven't noticed anything."
Patient denies prior similar episodes: "Has this happened before?" Patient: "No, no, I haven't noticed that before. I don't have any, like, history of... seeing this."

Osteoarthritis diagnosed by GP a few years ago: Patient: "I think I have something like osteoarthritis..." Doctor asks if a doctor confirmed; Patient: "Yes, a few years ago." and clarifies it was a GP.
Other illnesses denied: Doctor: "And do you have any other illnesses at all?" Patient: "Well, not really."
No eczema: Doctor asks, "Do you suffer from eczema at all?" Patient: "No."
No regular medications: Doctor: "are you on any medication on a regular basis?" Patient: "No, no."
Ibuprofen regimen given with GI caveat: "I would take ibuprofen regularly... 400 milligrams, three times a day... after food... If you get any heartburn, stop taking it."
Peanut allergy stated: Patient: "I'M allergic to. To peanuts."
No known family history of rheumatic disease: Doctor asks about family rheumatology diseases; Patient: "in my family, I'm not sure" indicating no known history.
Desk job: Doctor asks about physical work; Patient: "Not really, no. I just, you know, sit at the desk."
Runs 2–3 times per week and active: Patient: "I do do some sports. I run regularly. Like two, three times a week... I think I'm healthy."
Independence in ADLs reasonably inferred from being "normally fit and well, mobile, active" and running regularly with no mention of assistance.

Left elbow swelling, mild warmth, dry skin at tip: Assessment involves visualizing elbow; patient confirms "It's a bit warm" and doctor notes "the skin was a bit dry on the tip of the elbow." Swelling is described by the patient and accepted by the doctor.
Tenderness adjacent to swelling, not on tip: Patient: "On the tip of the elbow? It's okay. Just like next to it, like where the swelling is? It's a bit..."

No marked erythema and no significant pain on palpation are consistent with description: patient says "It's not painful at all" and only mild tenderness next to the tip; doctor notes it does not look like septic arthritis and never describes redness, implying absence of marked erythema.

Assessed as bursitis (likely olecranon bursitis): Doctor: "This seems like what we call the bursitis. Okay. So that's an inflammation of one of the fluid sacs around the joint." In the context of elbow, this corresponds to olecranon bursitis.
No evidence of septic arthritis: "your joint doesn't look like that" referring to "something called... septic arthritis" and noting current presentation is not that.
Past medical history includes osteoarthritis: as per pmh-001, confirmed GP diagnosis a few years ago.

Plan to start ibuprofen 400 mg TID with food and stop if GI symptoms: "I would take ibuprofen regularly... 400 milligrams, three times a day... after food... If you get any heartburn, stop taking it."

Blood tests ordered: "get some blood tests done to check for other types of causes of joint swelling... inflammatory markers, infection, rheumatological antibodies... and also check for things like gout as well" (gout → urate).
Forms to be sent: "we're going to arrange some blood test forms to be sent out to your house."

Follow-up around 6 days to review joint and results, can be virtual or in-person: Doctor explains results back in about 5–6 days and suggests follow-up where they "have a look at your joint, feel it, we can review the blood tests"; later: "follow up appointment doesn't have to be face to face... over the phone or video." Timing "maybe six days" is explicitly mentioned.

Safety-net advice for worsening redness/pain: Doctor: "if the elbow was to become very red, very painful, and the redness was to spread or become more intense, then you need to get on the phone or have a video appointment... as soon as possible because that would be an emergency."

Follow-up virtual or in-person after tests to review joint and results in ~6 days: matches plan-004 description of timeframe (~6 days), flexibility of format, and purpose (review elbow and blood tests).
